prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching 10^-18 fractional uncertainty and opening new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a measurement advance in the strict sense: the magic-wavelength condition removes the first-order light shift, Doppler and recoil effects while keeping thousands of atoms interrogated in parallel, and that combination is what took systematic uncertainty from the cesium-fountain level to about 10^-18. It is verified rather than proposed, since several independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) have built clocks and compared them at or beyond that level. It has already changed what can be measured: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, relativistic geodesy, and a concrete route to redefining the second. It has the broadest support in the opening round (two first places, four top-three rankings, eight of eight members ranking it). Katori (concept and first demonstration) and Ye (driving it to the accuracy frontier and the many-body spin-resolved clock physics) form a clean pair, with no need to stretch the three-person limit or to adjudicate a large collaboration.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are about novelty relative to earlier prizes and about priority. The 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion-based quantum control and clocks) already cover much of the enabling machinery, and a skeptical colleague can say lattice clocks are a very impressive refinement of a recognised program rather than a new discovery. Trapped-ion optical clocks (and Al+ clocks) reached comparable accuracy earlier or in parallel, and the lattice-clock priority also involves contributions from other groups (for instance Takamoto and the early Sr lattice work, Ludlow, Bloom, Campbell, and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST teams) that the two credited names do not fully represent. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the impact is still prospective, and the fundamental-physics results so far are limits rather than a discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator first, as a clear, original concept where theory and measured transport match quantitatively, with nearly two decades of independent confirmation, and he ranks the clock sixth.
responses.response: I agree B018 is mature and conceptually clean, and I put it forward as an alternative. My reservation is attribution and overlap: Eriksson himself notes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp's group then realised, and the three-person limit makes it hard to credit the full chain from Z2 classification to the first experiment. The 2016 prize on topological phases also covers adjacent ground. The clock case needs no such trade-off. I would not demote the clocks for being engineering-driven; the magic-wavelength idea is a physics idea that happens to be an instrument, and the measurement it enables is quantitatively unambiguous.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for its simple, general band-flattening mechanism and the clean pairing of the Bistritzer-MacDonald theory with the Jarillo-Herrero experiment.
responses.response: The flat-band mechanism is elegant, and the 2018 observations were reproduced quickly, which I respect. But Mehlig's own maturity note concedes that the nature of the superconductivity is still debated, and I would add that device-to-device variability and twist-angle disorder still limit reproducibility of the phase diagram. Olsson also flags that Yuan Cao, first author of the decisive experiments, is outside the credited trio. The clocks have been reproduced and improved by many groups over about two decades with stable interpretation. I see B022 as a strong candidate for a few years from now rather than clearly the better choice this year, though I would not object to it as a second part if the configuration allowed it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery first as the experimental completion of the Standard Model, without a prize of its own, and ranks the clocks seventh.
responses.response: I fully accept the scientific weight of the Higgs observation and its maturity, and I do not think the committee should ignore it. My difficulty is the attribution that Danielsson himself describes: thousands of contributors across two experiments, and a three-name limit that forces a choice between ATLAS and CMS leaders with Virdee, Gianotti, Jenni and Della Negra all defensible. Any trio looks like a compromise to the community. That is a reason for caution about making it the preferred prize now, not a reason to rank it lower on merit. If the committee settles the individual allocation, B055 is a serious rival to the clocks and I would want to see how colleagues divide the credit.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery that opened a new observational window, and he also places the optical lattice clock fourth as a natural Katori-Ye pairing.
responses.response: I share Pearce's values on instrument-driven discovery, and the diffuse flux is well established. The difference is in how complete the new window is: source identification still rests on a handful of objects (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane), so the astrophysical interpretation is maturing rather than mature, and the earlier DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA contributions complicate the two-name credit. Pearce's own maturity note says source identification is partial. I would therefore still place the clocks ahead on maturity and on clean attribution, while treating B013 as a good candidate for the near future.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first, emphasising quantitative agreement between theory and experiment, independent reproduction in many laboratories, and a clean two-laureate configuration.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and as an atomic physicist she is better placed than I am to judge the theory side of clock shifts. Where I would like to push is the interaction of the lattice clock with the ion-clock and comb prizes: we should make sure the citation speaks of the lattice-clock architecture and the 10^-18 regime, not of clocks in general, so that the novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 is explicit. Her second choice, antihydrogen (B059), is an impressive experimental program, but with no symmetry violation seen I weigh it as a precision null test rather than a discovery.

uncertainties: How much novelty the committee will grant relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and whether the citation can be worded to make the lattice-clock contribution distinct.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names, given priority and contribution questions involving other lattice-clock groups and parallel ion-clock work at similar accuracy.
Whether the pending decision on redefining the second matters for timing; I lean to treating the measured 10^-18 performance as sufficient.
Whether a clock prize combined with a second part (outside this union limit of three names) would be stronger than the single achievement.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. Lund atomic physics is in the same broad community as precision spectroscopy, and I once spent a year in John Hall's lab in Boulder (Hall is an earlier laureate and in the JILA/frequency-comb lineage adjacent to Ye), but I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye and see no recusal need; the committee may note it.
